beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here are two angles, A and B. Each one is made of two rays that start at the same point.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Which one is bigger?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: A! Look how long its rays are!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Let us trim the rays of A, down to the same length as B.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now, which one opens wider?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: B. It opens much wider. So the rays do not matter?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Right. An angle is not measured by its rays. It is measured by its turn. Let us watch one turn.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two rays lie one on top of the other, starting from one point. That point is the vertex.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One ray stays still. The other one turns.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: As it turns, it sweeps out space behind it. Let us count the turn, in degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten. Twenty. Thirty. Forty. Fifty. Sixty.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: It stops. The turn from one ray to the other is sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Turn on. At ninety degrees, the ray stands straight up. A square corner.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: At one hundred eighty degrees, the two rays make a straight line.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And at three hundred sixty degrees, it has gone all the way round, back to where it began. One full turn.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So one degree must be a really tiny piece of the way round!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes! Look closely at one degree. It is a sliver of turn, this thin.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Lay ten slivers side by side, and you have ten degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A full turn holds three hundred sixty of these slivers. That is why a full turn is three hundred sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three hundred sixty tiny turns!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So the measure of an angle just counts the slivers inside it. Sixty slivers, sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Back to sixty degrees. Now stretch both rays longer.

do.text: Change the rays. Not the turn.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now squeeze them shorter.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The fan does not change. The count does not change. Sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: It is the same angle. Only the rays got longer and shorter!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So the size of an angle is how far one ray has turned from the other. Nothing else.

do.text: Size of an angle = how far one ray has $\textbf{turned}$

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Counting slivers one at a time is slow. A protractor is half a turn, with the degrees already counted for us.

do.text: A protractor: half a turn, counted

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Put its center on the vertex, and its zero line along the ray that stayed still.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two scales run opposite ways. Start at the zero that sits on the still ray.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Follow that scale to the other ray. Twenty, forty, sixty. Sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: But I read one hundred twenty!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is the other scale. It started from the other side, so its zero is not on our still ray. It does not count the turn we made.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The rule: use the zero that sits on the still ray.

do.text: Start at the $\textbf{0}$ on the still ray. Stay on that scale.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now an angle that opens the other way. The still ray points left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The zero on that ray belongs to the other scale. So we use that one. Follow it to the other ray: forty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So I look for the zero on the still ray first. The scale comes after.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Always. And when a question says, use this ray as zero, that ray is the still ray. Find the scale that starts there.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Before you trust a reading, ask: does it make sense? Compare with a square corner. That is ninety degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This angle is narrower than a square corner. So it must be less than ninety. One hundred twenty could not be right.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Benchmarks help you estimate. Half a square corner is forty five degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut the square corner into three equal turns, and you get thirty degrees, and sixty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So I can tell thirty from sixty just by looking.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Sometimes you are told an angle is a fraction of the full turn. Then divide the three hundred sixty.

do.text: A fraction of a full turn

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut the turn into four equal parts. One quarter. Three hundred sixty divided by four is ninety.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut it into six equal parts instead. One sixth. Three hundred sixty divided by six is sixty.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Our sixty degrees is exactly one sixth of the way round!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Angles that sit side by side, sharing a ray, do not overlap. So their measures add.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is thirty five degrees. Next to it, fifty five degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Together they fill a square corner. Thirty five plus fifty five is ninety.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: The whole angle is just the parts added up.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now the whole angle is one hundred twenty degrees. One part is forty five degrees.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The other part we do not know yet. Call it *x*.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The parts add up to the whole. *x* plus forty five equals one hundred twenty.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: To find *x*, take the part we know away from the whole. One hundred twenty minus forty five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So *x* is seventy five degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And it looks right. It is less than a square corner.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One more. Sometimes two rays are drawn on one protractor, and neither sits on zero.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Read both from the same scale. One ray reads thirty. The other reads one hundred ten.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The angle between them is the difference. One hundred ten minus thirty is eighty degrees.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Each reading counts the turn from zero, so I take away the first thirty.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So here is the whole idea. An angle is a turn. A degree is one tiny sliver of a full turn, three hundred sixty to the way round.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A protractor counts those slivers for you. Not by how long the rays are. By how far the turn goes.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Start at zero on one ray. Read the turn to the other.
